# LAM Virtual Machine Specification

This document is the concrete, bit-level specification for the Logic
Abstract Machine (LAM). It is the single reference for implementers.
Higher-level rationale lives in `architecture.md` and `design.md`.

---

## 1. Tagged Cell Encoding

Every value in the LAM is a **24-bit tagged cell**. The top 3 bits are
the tag; the low 21 bits are the payload.

```
  23  22  21  20                                    0
 +---+---+---+--------------------------------------+
 | T   T   T |           payload (21 bits)           |
 +---+---+---+--------------------------------------+
```

### 1.1 Tag Values

| Tag | Binary | Decimal | Meaning                        |
|-----|--------|---------|--------------------------------|
| REF | `000`  | 0       | Variable reference (heap addr) |
| INT | `001`  | 1       | Small signed integer           |
| ATOM| `010`  | 2       | Interned atom ID               |
| STR | `011`  | 3       | Structure pointer (heap addr)  |
| LIST| `100`  | 4       | List cons-cell pointer (heap)  |
| FUN | `101`  | 5       | Functor header (name + arity)  |
| --- | `110`  | 6       | (reserved)                     |
| --- | `111`  | 7       | (reserved)                     |

### 1.2 Payload Semantics

| Tag  | Payload contains                                      |
|------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| REF  | Heap address of the referenced cell (0..2097151)      |
| INT  | 21-bit two's-complement integer (-1048576..1048575)   |
| ATOM | Atom-table index (0..2097151)                         |
| STR  | Heap address of the functor header cell                |
| LIST | Heap address of the first of two consecutive cells    |
| FUN  | Bits 20..5 = atom ID (16 bits), bits 4..0 = arity (5 bits) |

**FUN cells** appear only on the heap as structure headers. They are
never passed in registers directly — registers hold STR cells that
*point to* FUN cells.

**REF self-reference**: an unbound variable is a REF cell whose payload
points to its own heap address. Dereferencing follows REF chains until
it finds a self-referencing REF (unbound) or a non-REF cell (bound).

### 1.3 Masks and Shifts

```
TAG_BITS    = 3
TAG_SHIFT   = 21
TAG_MASK    = 0x700000     (bits 23-21)
PAYLOAD_MASK= 0x1FFFFF     (bits 20-0)
```

To extract:
- `tag     = (cell >> 21) & 0x7`
- `payload = cell & 0x1FFFFF`

To construct:
- `cell = (tag << 21) | (payload & 0x1FFFFF)`

For INT sign extension (21-bit two's complement):
- If bit 20 is set, the integer is negative.
- `value = payload | 0xFFE00000` when bit 20 is 1 (sign-extend to host width).

For FUN payload:
- `atom_id = (payload >> 5) & 0xFFFF`
- `arity   = payload & 0x1F`

### 1.4 Examples

| Term              | Tag  | Payload    | 24-bit hex   |
|-------------------|------|------------|--------------|
| Unbound var @ 5   | REF  | 5          | `0x000005`   |
| Integer 42        | INT  | 42         | `0x20002A`   |
| Integer -1        | INT  | 0x1FFFFF   | `0x3FFFFF`   |
| Atom `bob` (id=1) | ATOM | 1          | `0x400001`   |
| Struct ptr @ 10   | STR  | 10         | `0x60000A`   |
| List ptr @ 20     | LIST | 20         | `0x800014`   |
| Functor `f/2` (atom 3, arity 2) | FUN | (3<<5)\|2 = 0x62 | `0xA00062` |

### 1.5 Design Notes

- **Why 3-bit tag?** 8 tag slots are enough for all term types plus
  two reserved slots for future use (e.g., float approximation,
  special marker). The 21-bit payload gives 2M addressable heap cells,
  which is generous for an educational system on COR24.
- **Why separate STR and LIST?** Lists are extremely common in Prolog.
  A dedicated tag avoids the overhead of checking a functor header for
  `'.'/ 2` on every list operation.
- **Why FUN on heap only?** Keeping functor headers out of registers
  simplifies the register-level invariant: a register always holds a
  term you can unify against, never internal metadata.

---

## 2. Memory Map

The LAM divides its address space into eight contiguous regions. All
regions are measured in **cells** (24-bit words), not bytes. Addresses
in this document are cell indices.

### 2.1 Region Layout

```
Address (cell)   Size     Region
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
0x0000           256      Code area
0x0100           128      Atom table
0x0180           128      Functor table
0x0200            24      Register file
0x0218          4096      Heap
0x1218          1024      Trail
0x1618          1024      Environment stack
0x1A18          1024      Choice-point stack
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
0x1E18                    (end — total 7704 cells)
```

All sizes are defaults and defined as named constants so they can be
tuned without changing any other part of the spec.

### 2.2 Region Definitions

| Region             | Purpose                                                |
|--------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| Code area          | Compiled/assembled bytecode. Read-only at runtime.     |
| Atom table         | Maps atom ID -> name string (or hash). Entry 0 = `[]`. |
| Functor table      | Maps functor ID -> (atom_id, arity).                   |
| Register file      | A0-A7, X0-X7, special registers (see 2.3).             |
| Heap               | Term allocation. Grows upward from base. HP tracks top.|
| Trail              | Undo log for variable bindings. Grows upward. TR tracks top.|
| Environment stack  | Call frames for non-tail predicates. Grows upward. EP tracks top.|
| Choice-point stack | Backtracking state snapshots. Grows upward. BP tracks top.|

### 2.3 Register File Layout

The register file occupies 24 consecutive cells starting at `REG_BASE`
(0x0200). Each register is one cell-width slot.

```
Offset  Register   Role
──────────────────────────────────
 0      A0         Argument 0
 1      A1         Argument 1
 2      A2         Argument 2
 3      A3         Argument 3
 4      A4         Argument 4
 5      A5         Argument 5
 6      A6         Argument 6
 7      A7         Argument 7
 8      X0         Temporary 0
 9      X1         Temporary 1
10      X2         Temporary 2
11      X3         Temporary 3
12      X4         Temporary 4
13      X5         Temporary 5
14      X6         Temporary 6
15      X7         Temporary 7
16      PC         Program counter
17      CP         Continuation pointer
18      HP         Heap pointer (next free cell)
19      TR         Trail pointer (next free entry)
20      EP         Environment pointer
21      BP         Choice-point pointer
22      MODE       Unification mode (0=read, 1=write)
23      UP         Unification stream pointer
──────────────────────────────────
```

Register access: `mem[REG_BASE + offset]`.

Argument register `Ai` is at offset `i` (0-7).
Temporary register `Xi` is at offset `8 + i` (8-15).
Special registers start at offset 16.

### 2.4 Initial State

On VM reset:
- All registers zeroed.
- `HP` set to `HEAP_BASE` (0x0218).
- `TR` set to `TRAIL_BASE` (0x1218).
- `EP` set to `ENV_BASE` (0x1618).
- `BP` set to `CP_BASE` (0x1A18).
- `PC` set to 0 (start of code area).
- `MODE` set to 0 (read mode).
- Heap, trail, environment, and choice-point regions zeroed.

### 2.5 Design Notes

- **Why cell-addressed, not byte-addressed?** COR24 is a 24-bit word
  machine. Byte addressing would waste tag bits on alignment. Cell
  addressing keeps pointers compact within 21-bit payloads.
- **Why fixed-base regions?** Simplicity. No dynamic allocation of
  regions, no segment registers. A production system might use a more
  flexible layout, but for an educational VM, fixed bases make
  debugging and tracing straightforward.
- **Growth direction**: All dynamic regions (heap, trail, env stack,
  choice-point stack) grow upward. Overflow is detected by comparing
  the pointer against `BASE + SIZE`.
- **Total footprint**: ~7.7K cells. At 24 bits per cell, that is
  ~23 KB — well within COR24's reach.

; opcodes.plsw — Opcode constants for the LAM
;
; Each instruction is 1 or 2 cells wide. Cell 1 layout:
;   bits 23-16: opcode (8 bits)
;   bits 15-8:  operand1 (8 bits, typically register index)
;   bits  7-0:  operand2 (8 bits, typically register index)
;
; 2-cell instructions have a 24-bit immediate in cell 2.
;
; See docs/vm-spec.md section 3 for the full specification.

; --- Control (0-5) ---

OP_NOP          EQU 0       ; 1-cell  no operation
OP_HALT         EQU 1       ; 1-cell  stop execution
OP_CALL         EQU 2       ; 2-cell  call [imm]; CP = PC+2
OP_EXECUTE      EQU 3       ; 2-cell  tail-call [imm]
OP_PROCEED      EQU 4       ; 1-cell  return to CP
OP_FAIL         EQU 5       ; 1-cell  force backtracking

; --- Choice (6-9) ---

OP_TRY          EQU 6       ; 2-cell  push choice point; alt = [imm]
OP_RETRY        EQU 7       ; 2-cell  update alt to [imm]; retry
OP_TRUST        EQU 8       ; 1-cell  pop choice point; last alt

; --- PUT family (10-15) ---

OP_PUT_VAR      EQU 10      ; 1-cell  new var on heap; ref in Xn, Ai
OP_PUT_VAL      EQU 11      ; 1-cell  copy Xn to Ai
OP_PUT_CONST    EQU 12      ; 2-cell  load tagged [imm] into Ai

; --- GET family (16-21) ---

OP_GET_VAR      EQU 16      ; 1-cell  copy Ai to Xn
OP_GET_VAL      EQU 17      ; 1-cell  unify Xn with Ai
OP_GET_CONST    EQU 18      ; 2-cell  unify Ai with tagged [imm]
OP_GET_STRUCT   EQU 19      ; 2-cell  unify Ai with struct; functor [imm]

; --- UNIFY family (22-27) ---

OP_UNIFY_VAR    EQU 22      ; 1-cell  unify next heap arg with var Xn
OP_UNIFY_VAL    EQU 23      ; 1-cell  unify next heap arg with val Xn
OP_UNIFY_CONST  EQU 24      ; 2-cell  unify next heap arg with [imm]

; --- Frame management (28-31) ---

OP_ALLOCATE     EQU 28      ; 1-cell  allocate env frame (n slots)
OP_DEALLOCATE   EQU 29      ; 1-cell  pop env frame; restore CP

; --- Builtins (32-63) ---

OP_B_WRITE      EQU 32      ; 1-cell  print term in Ai
OP_B_NL         EQU 33      ; 1-cell  print newline

; --- Instruction encoding helpers ---

; opcodes.plsw — Opcode constants for the LAM
;
; Each instruction is 1 or 2 cells wide. Cell 1 layout:
;   bits 23-16: opcode (8 bits)
;   bits 15-8:  operand1 (8 bits, typically register index)
;   bits  7-0:  operand2 (8 bits, typically register index)
;
; 2-cell instructions have a 24-bit immediate in cell 2.
;
; See docs/vm-spec.md section 3 for the full specification.

; --- Control (0-5) ---

OP_NOP          EQU 0       ; 1-cell  no operation
OP_HALT         EQU 1       ; 1-cell  stop execution
OP_CALL         EQU 2       ; 2-cell  call [imm]; CP = PC+2
OP_EXECUTE      EQU 3       ; 2-cell  tail-call [imm]
OP_PROCEED      EQU 4       ; 1-cell  return to CP
OP_FAIL         EQU 5       ; 1-cell  force backtracking

; --- Choice (6-9) ---

OP_TRY          EQU 6       ; 2-cell  push choice point; alt = [imm]
OP_RETRY        EQU 7       ; 2-cell  update alt to [imm]; retry
OP_TRUST        EQU 8       ; 1-cell  pop choice point; last alt

; --- PUT family (10-15) ---

OP_PUT_VAR      EQU 10      ; 1-cell  new var on heap; ref in Xn, Ai
OP_PUT_VAL      EQU 11      ; 1-cell  copy Xn to Ai
OP_PUT_CONST    EQU 12      ; 2-cell  load tagged [imm] into Ai

; --- GET family (16-21) ---

OP_GET_VAR      EQU 16      ; 1-cell  copy Ai to Xn
OP_GET_VAL      EQU 17      ; 1-cell  unify Xn with Ai
OP_GET_CONST    EQU 18      ; 2-cell  unify Ai with tagged [imm]
OP_GET_STRUCT   EQU 19      ; 2-cell  unify Ai with struct; functor [imm]

; --- UNIFY family (22-27) ---

OP_UNIFY_VAR    EQU 22      ; 1-cell  unify next heap arg with var Xn
OP_UNIFY_VAL    EQU 23      ; 1-cell  unify next heap arg with val Xn
OP_UNIFY_CONST  EQU 24      ; 2-cell  unify next heap arg with [imm]

; --- Frame management (28-31) ---

OP_ALLOCATE     EQU 28      ; 1-cell  allocate env frame (n slots)
OP_DEALLOCATE   EQU 29      ; 1-cell  pop env frame; restore CP

; --- Builtins (32-63) ---

OP_B_WRITE      EQU 32      ; 1-cell  print term in Ai
OP_B_NL         EQU 33      ; 1-cell  print newline

; --- Instruction encoding helpers ---
;
; Build instruction cell:
;   (opcode << 16) | (op1 << 8) | op2
;
; Decode:
;   opcode = (cell >> 16) & 0xFF
;   op1    = (cell >> 8)  & 0xFF
;   op2    = cell & 0xFF

OP_SHIFT        EQU 16
OP1_SHIFT       EQU 8
OP_FIELD_MASK   EQU 0xFF

# sw-cor24-prolog

A clean-room Prolog project for the COR24 ecosystem.

## Approach

This project takes a VM-first path:

1. Build a WAM-like VM in PL/SW
2. Give the VM:
   - 8 argument registers: `A0..A7`
   - 8 temporary registers: `X0..X7`
3. Run that VM on COR24
4. Build Tiny Prolog on top of the VM

The goal is educational clarity first, then practical experimentation.

- `docs/architecture.md`
- `docs/prd.md`
- `docs/design.md`
- `docs/plan.md`

#### Frame Management

| #  | Mnemonic    | Op1  | Op2 | Width | Description                              |
|----|-------------|------|-----|-------|------------------------------------------|
| 28 | ALLOCATE    | n    | —   | 1     | Allocate env frame with n local slots    |
| 29 | DEALLOCATE  | —    | —   | 1     | Pop env frame; restore CP from frame     |

#### Builtins

| #  | Mnemonic | Op1  | Op2 | Width | Description                              |
|----|----------|------|-----|-------|------------------------------------------|
| 32 | B_WRITE  | Ai   | —   | 1     | Print term in Ai                         |
| 33 | B_NL     | —    | —   | 1     | Print newline                            |

### 3.4 Opcode Numbering

Opcodes are grouped with gaps between categories to allow future
expansion without renumbering:

- 0-5: control
- 6-9: choice
- 10-15: PUT family
- 16-21: GET family
- 22-27: UNIFY family
- 28-31: frame management
- 32-63: builtins

### 3.5 Instruction Width Summary

**1-cell** (opcode + register operands only):
NOP, HALT, PROCEED, FAIL, TRUST, PUT_VAR, PUT_VAL, GET_VAR, GET_VAL,
UNIFY_VAR, UNIFY_VAL, ALLOCATE, DEALLOCATE, B_WRITE, B_NL.

**2-cell** (opcode + immediate in cell 2):
CALL, EXECUTE, TRY, RETRY, PUT_CONST, GET_CONST, GET_STRUCT,
UNIFY_CONST.

### 3.6 Design Notes

- **Why 8-bit opcode?** 256 slots is far more than needed, but the
  uniform 8-bit field keeps decoding trivial: `opcode = cell >> 16`.
  No variable-length opcode decoding.
- **Why gaps in numbering?** Adding a `PUT_STRUCT` (13) or `PUT_LIST`
  (14) later doesn't force renumbering existing code.
- **Why full tagged cell for constants?** PUT_CONST and GET_CONST pass
  complete tagged cells as immediates. This means the assembler doesn't
  need separate "load atom" vs "load integer" opcodes — the tag in the
  immediate distinguishes them.
- **PC advance**: 1-cell instructions advance PC by 1. 2-cell
  instructions advance PC by 2. CALL saves PC+2 to CP (the cell after
  the immediate). PROCEED sets PC = CP.

- **PC advance**: 1-cell instructions advance PC by 1. 2-cell
  instructions advance PC by 2. CALL saves PC+2 to CP (the cell after
  the immediate). PROCEED sets PC = CP.

---

## 4. Frame and Entry Layouts

### 4.1 Choice-Point Frame

Stored on the choice-point stack. Each frame is a **fixed 14-cell
block**. BP points to the base (offset 0) of the most recent frame.

```
Offset  Field       Contents
──────────────────────────────────────────
 0      prev_BP     Previous choice-point address (or CP_BASE if none)
 1      saved_CP    Continuation pointer at time of TRY
 2      saved_EP    Environment pointer at time of TRY
 3      saved_HP    Heap pointer at time of TRY
 4      saved_TR    Trail pointer at time of TRY
 5      next_alt    Code address of next alternative clause
 6      saved_A0    Argument register A0
 7      saved_A1    Argument register A1
 8      saved_A2    Argument register A2
 9      saved_A3    Argument register A3
10      saved_A4    Argument register A4
11      saved_A5    Argument register A5
12      saved_A6    Argument register A6
13      saved_A7    Argument register A7
──────────────────────────────────────────
Total: 14 cells
```

**TRY** creates a frame:
1. Write all 14 fields at `BP`.
2. Advance `BP` by 14 (new BP = old BP + `CP_FRAME_SIZE`).

**RETRY** updates the current frame:
1. Restore A0-A7, HP, TR from the frame at `BP - 14`.
2. Unwind trail entries from current TR back to `saved_TR`.
3. Update `next_alt` to the new alternative address.
4. Resume execution at the alternative.

**TRUST** pops the frame:
1. Restore A0-A7, HP, TR from the frame at `BP - 14`.
2. Unwind trail entries.
3. Set `BP` = `prev_BP` (pop the frame).
4. Resume execution at `next_alt`.

**Backtracking on FAIL**:
1. If `BP` == `CP_BASE`, no choice points remain — execution fails.
2. Otherwise, behave like TRUST on the current frame.

### 4.2 Environment Frame

Stored on the environment stack. Each frame is **2 + N cells**, where
N is the number of local variables (the operand to ALLOCATE).

```
Offset  Field       Contents
──────────────────────────────────────────
 0      prev_EP     Previous environment pointer (or ENV_BASE if none)
 1      saved_CP    Continuation pointer to restore on DEALLOCATE
 2      Y0          Local variable 0
 3      Y1          Local variable 1
 ...    ...         ...
 1+N    Y(N-1)      Local variable N-1
──────────────────────────────────────────
Total: 2 + N cells
```

**ALLOCATE n**:
1. Write `prev_EP` = current EP value, `saved_CP` = current CP value
   at the address pointed to by EP.
2. Initialize Y0..Y(N-1) to unbound REF cells (self-referencing, using
   their heap-independent stack addresses — or left zeroed for lazy init).
3. Advance EP by `2 + N`.

**DEALLOCATE**:
1. Read `saved_CP` from the frame at `EP - (2 + N)` and restore CP.
2. Read `prev_EP` and restore EP.

Note: the frame size N is not stored in the frame itself. The compiler
knows N for each predicate and emits matching ALLOCATE/DEALLOCATE pairs.
At runtime, DEALLOCATE can recover the frame base because EP still
points past the current frame — the previous EP at `prev_EP` gives the
correct restore point. Implementation may store N at a known offset or
track it via the compiler's metadata; the simplest approach is to save
the current EP at ALLOCATE time and restore it at DEALLOCATE:

- ALLOCATE saves `old_EP` into the frame, then sets EP = `old_EP + 2 + N`.
- DEALLOCATE sets EP = frame base (by reading `prev_EP` would be wrong —
  we need the frame's own base). The simplest encoding: EP always points
  to the **base** of the current frame, and a separate pointer or the
  saved value tracks the next free slot. For this VM, we adopt the
  convention:

  **EP points to the base of the current environment frame.**

  ALLOCATE: write frame at `next_env` (tracked as EP + frame_size of
  current frame, or via a running env-top pointer). For simplicity in
  this first VM, ALLOCATE writes at the current env-top, and EP is set
  to that address. A separate `ET` (env top) register could track the
  next free cell, but to keep the register count small, we compute it:
  `env_top = EP + 2 + N` after ALLOCATE.

  For the initial implementation, the simplest correct approach:
  - EP points to the **base** of the most recent frame.
  - The frame stores `prev_EP` so DEALLOCATE can restore it.
  - The next ALLOCATE writes at `EP + 2 + N` (caller knows N).

### 4.3 Trail Entries

Each trail entry is **1 cell**: the absolute heap address of a variable
that was bound during forward execution.

```
Trail stack (grows upward from TRAIL_BASE):

 TR-1  →  heap_addr    ← most recent binding
 TR-2  →  heap_addr
 ...
 TRAIL_BASE → heap_addr ← oldest binding
```

**Trailing** (during bind):
1. Store the heap address at `mem[TR]`.
2. Increment TR by 1.

**Unwinding** (during backtrack to saved_TR):
1. For each entry from `TR-1` down to `saved_TR`:
   - Read heap address `H` from the trail entry.
   - Reset `mem[H]` to `(TAG_REF << TAG_SHIFT) | H` (self-referencing
     REF — unbinds the variable).
2. Set `TR` = `saved_TR`.

**Conditional trailing**: a binding only needs to be trailed if the
variable's heap address is older than the current choice point's
`saved_HP`. Variables created after the choice point will be reclaimed
when HP is reset, so trailing them is unnecessary. This optimization is
deferred to a later milestone — the initial VM trails all bindings
unconditionally.

### 4.4 Design Notes

- **Why save all 8 argument registers in choice points?** Simplicity.
  A production WAM saves only the registers actually used by the
  predicate (determined at compile time). Saving all 8 wastes a few
  cells per choice point but eliminates a source of compiler bugs in
  the first milestone.
- **Why no frame-size field in environment frames?** The compiler
  emits matched ALLOCATE/DEALLOCATE pairs, so N is always known
  statically. Storing it would add a cell per frame for no runtime
  benefit.
- **Why 1-cell trail entries?** Binding always sets a REF cell to
  point to another cell. On undo, we just need to know which address
  to reset to self-referencing. The old value is always "unbound REF
  at that address" — no need to store it.

 0      prev_EP     Previous environment pointer (or ENV_BASE if none)
 1      saved_CP    Continuation pointer to restore on DEALLOCATE
 2      Y0          Local variable 0
 3      Y1          Local variable 1
 ...    ...         ...
 1+N    Y(N-1)      Local variable N-1
──────────────────────────────────────────
Total: 2 + N cells
```

**ALLOCATE n**:
1. Write `prev_EP` = current EP value, `saved_CP` = current CP value
   at the address pointed to by EP.
2. Initialize Y0..Y(N-1) to unbound REF cells (self-referencing, using
   their heap-independent stack addresses — or left zeroed for lazy init).
3. Advance EP by `2 + N`.

**DEALLOCATE**:
1. Read `saved_CP` from the frame at `EP - (2 + N)` and restore CP.
2. Read `prev_EP` and restore EP.

Note: the frame size N is not stored in the frame itself. The compiler
knows N for each predicate and emits matching ALLOCATE/DEALLOCATE pairs.
At runtime, DEALLOCATE can recover the frame base because EP still
points past the current frame — the previous EP at `prev_EP` gives the
correct restore point. Implementation may store N at a known offset or
track it via the compiler's metadata; the simplest approach is to save
the current EP at ALLOCATE time and restore it at DEALLOCATE:

- ALLOCATE saves `old_EP` into the frame, then sets EP = `old_EP + 2 + N`.
- DEALLOCATE sets EP = frame base (by reading `prev_EP` would be wrong —
  we need the frame's own base). The simplest encoding: EP always points
  to the **base** of the current frame, and a separate pointer or the
  saved value tracks the next free slot. For this VM, we adopt the
  convention:

  **EP points to the base of the current environment frame.**

  ALLOCATE: write frame at `next_env` (tracked as EP + frame_size of
  current frame, or via a running env-top pointer). For simplicity in
  this first VM, ALLOCATE writes at the current env-top, and EP is set
  to that address. A separate `ET` (env top) register could track the
  next free cell, but to keep the register count small, we compute it:
  `env_top = EP + 2 + N` after ALLOCATE.

  For the initial implementation, the simplest correct approach:
  - EP points to the **base** of the most recent frame.
  - The frame stores `prev_EP` so DEALLOCATE can restore it.
  - The next ALLOCATE writes at `EP + 2 + N` (caller knows N).

### 4.3 Trail Entries

Each trail entry is **1 cell**: the absolute heap address of a variable
that was bound during forward execution.

```
Trail stack (grows upward from TRAIL_BASE):

 TR-1  →  heap_addr    ← most recent binding
 TR-2  →  heap_addr
 ...
 TRAIL_BASE → heap_addr ← oldest binding
```

**Trailing** (during bind):
1. Store the heap address at `mem[TR]`.
2. Increment TR by 1.

**Unwinding** (during backtrack to saved_TR):
1. For each entry from `TR-1` down to `saved_TR`:
   - Read heap address `H` from the trail entry.
   - Reset `mem[H]` to `(TAG_REF << TAG_SHIFT) | H` (self-referencing
     REF — unbinds the variable).
2. Set `TR` = `saved_TR`.

**Conditional trailing**: a binding only needs to be trailed if the
variable's heap address is older than the current choice point's
`saved_HP`. Variables created after the choice point will be reclaimed
when HP is reset, so trailing them is unnecessary. This optimization is
deferred to a later milestone — the initial VM trails all bindings
unconditionally.

  statically. Storing it would add a cell per frame for no runtime
  benefit.

  point to another cell. On undo, we just need to know which address
  to reset to self-referencing. The old value is always "unbound REF
  at that address" — no need to store it.

; opcodes.plsw — Opcode constants for the LAM
;
; Each instruction is 1 or 2 cells wide. Cell 1 layout:
;   bits 23-16: opcode (8 bits)
;   bits 15-8:  operand1 (8 bits, typically register index)
;   bits  7-0:  operand2 (8 bits, typically register index)
;
; 2-cell instructions have a 24-bit immediate in cell 2.
;
; See docs/vm-spec.md section 3 for the full specification.

; --- Control (0-5) ---

OP_NOP          EQU 0       ; 1-cell  no operation
OP_HALT         EQU 1       ; 1-cell  stop execution
OP_CALL         EQU 2       ; 2-cell  call [imm]; CP = PC+2
OP_EXECUTE      EQU 3       ; 2-cell  tail-call [imm]
OP_PROCEED      EQU 4       ; 1-cell  return to CP
OP_FAIL         EQU 5       ; 1-cell  force backtracking

; --- Choice (6-9) ---

OP_TRY          EQU 6       ; 2-cell  push choice point; alt = [imm]
OP_RETRY        EQU 7       ; 2-cell  update alt to [imm]; retry
OP_TRUST        EQU 8       ; 1-cell  pop choice point; last alt

; --- PUT family (10-15) ---

OP_PUT_VAR      EQU 10      ; 1-cell  new var on heap; ref in Xn, Ai
OP_PUT_VAL      EQU 11      ; 1-cell  copy Xn to Ai
OP_PUT_CONST    EQU 12      ; 2-cell  load tagged [imm] into Ai

; --- GET family (16-21) ---

OP_GET_VAR      EQU 16      ; 1-cell  copy Ai to Xn
OP_GET_VAL      EQU 17      ; 1-cell  unify Xn with Ai
OP_GET_CONST    EQU 18      ; 2-cell  unify Ai with tagged [imm]
OP_GET_STRUCT   EQU 19      ; 2-cell  unify Ai with struct; functor [imm]

; --- UNIFY family (22-27) ---

OP_UNIFY_VAR    EQU 22      ; 1-cell  unify next heap arg with var Xn
OP_UNIFY_VAL    EQU 23      ; 1-cell  unify next heap arg with val Xn
OP_UNIFY_CONST  EQU 24      ; 2-cell  unify next heap arg with [imm]

; --- Frame management (28-31) ---

OP_ALLOCATE     EQU 28      ; 1-cell  allocate env frame (n slots)
OP_DEALLOCATE   EQU 29      ; 1-cell  pop env frame; restore CP

; --- Builtins (32-63) ---

OP_B_WRITE      EQU 32      ; 1-cell  print term in Ai
OP_B_NL         EQU 33      ; 1-cell  print newline

;
; Build instruction cell:
;   (opcode << 16) | (op1 << 8) | op2
;

;   op1    = (cell >> 8)  & 0xFF

; cell.plsw — Tagged cell constants for the LAM
;
; Every value in the LAM is a 24-bit tagged cell:
;
;   [23..21] tag  (3 bits)  — term type
;   [20.. 0] payload (21 bits) — address, integer, or packed field
;
; See docs/vm-spec.md for the full specification.

; --- Tag values (top 3 bits) ---

TAG_REF     EQU 0           ; variable reference (heap address)
TAG_INT     EQU 1           ; small signed integer (21-bit two's complement)
TAG_ATOM    EQU 2           ; interned atom ID
TAG_STR     EQU 3           ; structure pointer (heap address of FUN header)
TAG_LIST    EQU 4           ; list cons-cell pointer (heap address)
TAG_FUN     EQU 5           ; functor header (atom_id << 5 | arity)
;           EQU 6           ; (reserved)
;           EQU 7           ; (reserved)

; --- Masks and shifts ---

TAG_SHIFT       EQU 21
TAG_MASK        EQU 0x700000   ; bits 23-21
PAYLOAD_MASK    EQU 0x1FFFFF   ; bits 20-0

; Functor payload sub-fields
FUN_ARITY_BITS  EQU 5
FUN_ARITY_MASK  EQU 0x1F       ; bits 4-0 of payload
FUN_ATOM_SHIFT  EQU 5          ; atom ID starts at bit 5 of payload

; --- Cell construction ---
;
; To build a cell:      (tag << TAG_SHIFT) | (payload & PAYLOAD_MASK)
; To extract tag:       (cell >> TAG_SHIFT) & 0x7
; To extract payload:   cell & PAYLOAD_MASK
;
; Functor payload:
;   Build:   (atom_id << FUN_ATOM_SHIFT) | arity
;   Arity:   payload & FUN_ARITY_MASK
;   Atom ID: (payload >> FUN_ATOM_SHIFT) & 0xFFFF

; --- Unbound variable convention ---
;
; An unbound variable at heap address H is stored as:
;   (TAG_REF << TAG_SHIFT) | H
;
; i.e., a REF cell that points to itself. Dereferencing follows
; REF chains until it reaches a self-referencing REF (unbound)
; or a non-REF cell (bound value).

# Demos

Hand-assembled bytecode examples for the LAM virtual machine. These
are static listings — no VM runtime exists yet to execute them. Each
file contains hex-encoded bytecode with mnemonic annotations and a
step-by-step execution trace showing what the VM *would* do.

## examples/ancestor/fact_lookup.asm

**Prolog equivalent:**

```prolog
parent(bob, ann).
?- parent(bob, ann).
```

Demonstrates the simplest possible LAM program: load two atom constants
into argument registers, call a single-clause predicate, match both
arguments, and halt on success. Exercises:

- `PUT_CONST` — load a tagged atom into an argument register
- `CALL` / `PROCEED` — predicate call and return via CP
- `GET_CONST` — head-argument matching against a constant
- `HALT` — clean termination

13 cells of bytecode. Linear execution, no branching or backtracking.

## examples/ancestor/two_facts.asm

**Prolog equivalent:**

```prolog
parent(bob, ann).
parent(bob, joe).
?- parent(bob, X), write(X), nl, fail.
```

Demonstrates choice points and backtracking. The query creates an
unbound variable for X, calls `parent/2` which has two clauses linked
by `TRY`/`TRUST`, prints each answer, then forces backtracking with
`FAIL` to find the next. Expected output:

```
ann
joe
```

Exercises (in addition to the above):

- `PUT_VAR` — create an unbound heap variable and reference it
- `TRY` / `TRUST` — choice-point creation and removal
- `FAIL` — forced backtracking

parent(bob, ann).
?- parent(bob, ann).

**Prolog equivalent:**

```prolog
parent(bob, ann).
parent(bob, joe).
?- parent(bob, X), write(X), nl, fail.
```

joe

# Development Tools

This document describes the recommended tools for working with this project, particularly for AI coding agents and developers.

## Tool Location

Recommended tools are installed in `~/.local/softwarewrighter/bin/`:

```bash
# List available tools
ls -la ~/.local/softwarewrighter/bin/

# Add to PATH (if not already in ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc)
export PATH="$HOME/.local/softwarewrighter/bin:$PATH"
```

## Tool Help Convention

**IMPORTANT**: All tools in `~/.local/softwarewrighter/bin/` support `--help` with AI coding agent-specific sections. These extended help sections provide additional context, examples, and best practices tailored for AI agents.

```bash
# Standard help (short)
tool-name -h

# Extended help with AI sections (recommended)
tool-name --help
```

## Core Tools

### 1. proact - AI Agent Documentation Generator

**Repository**: https://github.com/softwarewrighter/proact
**Version**: 0.1.0

**Purpose**: Generates comprehensive AI coding agent documentation for projects

**When to Use**:
- When starting work on a new project
- When you want standardized AI agent instructions
- When docs/learnings.md needs to be initialized or updated
- When project processes/standards have changed

**Installation**:
```bash
# Already installed in ~/.local/softwarewrighter/bin/
```

**Usage**:
```bash
# Generate docs for current project
proact .

# Generate docs for specific project
proact /path/to/project

# Custom output directory
proact /path/to/project -o documentation

# Preview what would be generated (dry-run)
proact . --dry-run

# Verbose output
proact . --verbose
```

**What It Generates**:
- `docs/ai_agent_instructions.md` - Comprehensive AI coding agent guidelines
  - Process-oriented workflow
  - Quality standards
  - Testing strategies
  - Tech debt avoidance
  - Playwright MCP setup
  - Project-specific guidelines (Rust, WASM, etc.)
- `docs/learnings.md` - Template for capturing issues and solutions
  - Common patterns that cause problems
  - Proactive prevention strategies
  - Root cause analysis examples

**Key Features**:
- Enforces checkpoint process (tests, linting, formatting, docs, git)
- Includes Playwright MCP setup instructions
- Project-specific guidelines based on technology detected
- Continuous improvement focus
- Tech debt limits (file size, TODO count, etc.)

**AI Agent Notes**:
When proact generates documentation for a project, it creates a baseline. You should:
1. Read the generated docs/ai_agent_instructions.md
2. Follow the checkpoint process it describes
3. Update docs/learnings.md when you encounter issues
4. Run proact again if project structure changes significantly

### 2. markdown-checker - Markdown Validation Tool

**Repository**: https://github.com/softwarewrighter/markdown-checker
**Version**: 0.1.0

**Purpose**: Ensures markdown files use ASCII-only characters for maximum portability

**When to Use**:
- BEFORE committing any markdown changes (part of pre-commit process)
- After editing README.md or any docs/*.md files
- When preparing documentation for GitHub (web preview compatibility)
- To fix Unicode characters (arrows, emojis, box-drawing)

**Installation**:
```bash
# Already installed in ~/.local/softwarewrighter/bin/
```

**Usage**:
```bash
# Validate README.md in current directory
markdown-checker

# Validate specific file
markdown-checker -f CONTRIBUTING.md

# Validate all markdown in directory
markdown-checker -f "*.md"

# Validate recursively (all markdown in docs/)
markdown-checker -p docs -f "**/*.md"

# Auto-fix tree symbols
markdown-checker --fix

# Preview fixes without applying
markdown-checker --dry-run

# Verbose output
markdown-checker -v
```

**Validation Rules**:
- [x] ASCII characters (32-126)
- [x] Whitespace (space, tab, LF, CR)
- [x] Unicode arrows (-> becomes ->)
- [x] Emojis ([x] becomes [x] or remove)
- [x] Box-drawing characters (+|+- becomes +|-)

**Auto-Fixable**:
- Tree symbols: `+ -> +`, `| -> |`, `+ -> +`, `- -> -`

**Not Auto-Fixable** (manual intervention required):
- Unicode arrows (->)
- Emojis ([x] [x] [WIP])
- Accented characters (e a n)
- Other non-ASCII Unicode

**Why ASCII-Only?**:
- GitHub README web preview works correctly
- Compatible with all terminals and editors
- Works in CI/CD pipelines
- Accessible to screen readers
- No encoding issues

**Pre-Commit Integration**:
```bash
# Part of mandatory pre-commit process
markdown-checker -f "**/*.md"
# Fix any issues before committing
```

**AI Agent Notes**:
- ALWAYS run markdown-checker before committing documentation
- Use --fix for tree symbols, manually fix other Unicode
- If validation fails, FIX the issues (never skip this step)
- Common fixes:
  - `->` becomes `->`
  - `[x]` becomes `[x]` in checklists
  - `[WIP]` becomes `[WIP]` or remove
  - Box-drawing trees become ASCII trees

### 3. sw-install - Binary Installation Tool

**Repository**: https://github.com/softwarewrighter/sw-install
**Version**: 0.1.0

**Purpose**: Installs compiled Rust binaries to `~/.local/softwarewrighter/bin/`

**When to Use**:
- First-time setup of development environment
- After building a new Rust CLI tool locally
- When updating an existing tool
- When you need a specific version of a tool

**Installation**:
```bash
# Already installed in ~/.local/softwarewrighter/bin/
```

**First-Time Setup**:
```bash
# 1. Setup installation directory and PATH
sw-install --setup-install-dir

# 2. Reload shell configuration
source ~/.bashrc  # or ~/.zshrc
```

**Usage**:
```bash
# Install a binary from project (release build)
sw-install -p ~/projects/markdown-checker

# Install with custom name
sw-install -p ~/projects/ask -r ask-dev

# Install debug build (for development)
sw-install -p ~/projects/proact -d

# Uninstall a binary
sw-install -u markdown-checker

# Dry-run (preview what would happen)
sw-install -p ~/projects/ask --dry-run

# Verbose output
sw-install -p ~/projects/ask --verbose
```

**How It Works**:
1. Detects Rust project (looks for Cargo.toml)
2. Finds binary name from Cargo.toml [[bin]] section
3. Copies from `target/release/` or `target/debug/`
4. Installs to `~/.local/softwarewrighter/bin/`
5. Makes executable (chmod +x)

**PATH Configuration**:
After `--setup-install-dir`, adds to your shell RC file:
```bash
export PATH="$HOME/.local/softwarewrighter/bin:$PATH"
```

**AI Agent Notes**:
- Use sw-install when you build a new tool and want it available globally
- Prefer release builds for performance: `sw-install -p <path>`
- Use debug builds for development: `sw-install -p <path> -d`
- Check which tools are available: `ls ~/.local/softwarewrighter/bin/`

### 4. ask - Command-Line LLM Query Tool

**Repository**: https://github.com/softwarewrighter/ask
**Version**: 0.1.0

**Purpose**: Query language models from the command line for quick assistance

**When to Use**:
- Need quick answers without opening a full AI interface
- Testing API integrations
- Generating code snippets
- Answering technical questions
- Prototyping prompts

**Installation**:
```bash
# Already installed in ~/.local/softwarewrighter/bin/
```

**Usage**:
```bash
# Query with default settings (Ollama, phi3:3.8b)
ask "How do I parse JSON in Rust?"

# Use a specific platform and model
ask -p openai -m gpt-4 "Explain async/await in Rust"

# Use shortcut for platform/model combo
ask -s  # List available shortcuts
ask -s sonnet "Write a bash script to..."

# Dry run (show request without calling API)
ask -n "Test query"

# Verbose output
ask -v "Debug query"

# Show usage statistics
ask --usage-report
```

**Supported Platforms**:
- Ollama (default, local)
- OpenAI (requires API key)
- Anthropic (requires API key)

**Configuration**:
```bash
# API keys via environment variables
export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."

# Or via config file
~/.config/ask/config.toml
```

**AI Agent Notes**:
- Useful for quick references without context switching
- Ollama is default (runs locally, no API costs)
- Set API keys in environment for OpenAI/Anthropic
- Use --usage-report to track API costs

### 5. sw-checklist - Software Wrighter Project Requirements Checker

**Repository**: https://github.com/softwarewrighter/sw-checklist
**Version**: 0.1.0

**Purpose**: Ensures that a project meets Software Wrighter standards and requirements

**When to Use**:
- Before committing changes to verify project compliance
- When setting up a new project to ensure all requirements are met
- During pre-commit process to validate project structure
- To identify missing or non-compliant project elements

**Installation**:
```bash
# Already installed in ~/.local/softwarewrighter/bin/
```

**Usage**:
```bash
# Run checklist on current project
sw-checklist

# Show extended help with AI agent guidance
sw-checklist --help

# Run with verbose output
sw-checklist -v

# Dry run (preview checks without modifications)
sw-checklist --dry-run
```

**What It Checks**:
- Project structure and required files
- Documentation completeness
- Code quality standards
- Testing requirements
- License and copyright information
- Build and deployment configuration

**AI Agent Notes**:
- Run sw-checklist before creating commits to ensure compliance
- Use --help to understand specific requirements for your project type
- Address all checklist failures before pushing to remote
- Integrate into pre-commit workflow for automated validation

### 6. favicon - Favicon Generator

**Repository**: https://github.com/softwarewrighter/favicon
**Version**: 0.1.0

**Purpose**: Generates favicon.ico files for web projects

**When to Use**:
- Setting up a new web project that needs a favicon
- Creating placeholder favicons during development
- Generating production-ready favicon files

**Installation**:
```bash
# Already installed in ~/.local/softwarewrighter/bin/
```

**Usage**:
```bash
# Show extended help with AI agent guidance
favicon --help

# Generate red question mark on transparent background (placeholder)
# Run this in the directory where index.html is served (e.g., public/ or static/)
favicon -T -t "?" -b ff0000

# Common options:
# -T          : Transparent background
# -t "TEXT"   : Text to render in favicon
# -b RRGGBB   : Background color (hex)
# -f RRGGBB   : Foreground/text color (hex)
```

**Common Patterns**:

```bash
# Placeholder during development (red question mark)
cd public  # or wherever index.html is served
favicon -T -t "?" -b ff0000

# Development marker (yellow "D")
favicon -T -t "D" -b ffff00 -f 000000

# Staging marker (orange "S")
favicon -T -t "S" -b ff8800 -f ffffff

# Production placeholder (blue "P")
favicon -T -t "P" -b 0066ff -f ffffff
```

**AI Agent Notes**:
- ALWAYS run favicon in the directory where index.html is served
- Common locations: public/, static/, dist/, www/
- Replace placeholder favicons before production deployment
- Use distinctive colors/text for different environments (dev/staging/prod)
- The -T flag creates transparent backgrounds for better visual appearance

5	Prolog clean-room implementation using my COR24 tools.  see: https://sw-embed.github.io/web-sw-cor24-demos/#/ -- How is Prolog usually implemented, bootstrapped?  I prefer building in PL/SW than C if possible, but if Prolog works better on p-code VM, then Pascal is okay (like how I implemented BASIC).  I could, theoretically implement Prolog in SNOBOL4 (like I am for Fortran).  The target machine has no divide, no floating point, 24-bit, 3 GPRs
6	
7	I’m checking the demo page you linked so I can ground the design around your actual COR24 toolchain and not answer too generically. Then I’ll map typical Prolog implementation strategies onto your constraints.
8	
9	Thought for 22s
10	You want a clean-room Prolog for COR24, using your existing toolchain where possible, under these constraints:
11	
12	Target: 24-bit machine, no divide, no floating point, only 3 general-purpose registers
13	
14	Preferred implementation language: PL/SW
15	
16	Fallbacks: Pascal on your p-code VM, or even SNOBOL4
17	
18	Goal: understand how Prolog is usually implemented and bootstrapped, then choose the path that best fits COR24
19	
20	The core design question is not really “What source language should I write it in?” but rather:
21	
22	Do you want to implement Prolog as
23	
24	a tree-walking interpreter,
25	
26	a bytecode VM, or
27	
28	a WAM-like compiler/runtime?
29	
30	That choice determines everything else.
31	
32	How Prolog is usually implemented
33	Classic Prolog systems are usually based on the Warren Abstract Machine (WAM) or a close relative. The WAM compiles Prolog clauses into a low-level instruction set and runs them on a runtime built around unification, choice points, backtracking, the trail, heap-allocated terms, and usually indexing on predicate arguments. Many later systems simplify or vary this, but the WAM became the standard mental model for Prolog implementation. 
34	
35	A simpler variant is to compile Prolog into a smaller abstract machine rather than a full classic WAM. SWI-Prolog’s implementation history explicitly describes using a much simpler VM (“ZIP”), noting that Prolog can be compiled into it and even decompiled back into Prolog, which is useful for debugging and reducing the gap between “interpreted” and “compiled” execution. 
36	
37	So the mainstream historical answer is:
38	
39	Early educational/simple systems: interpreter over clauses/terms
40	
41	Serious classic systems: WAM-style compiled runtime
42	
43	Portable or compact implementations: some smaller VM than full WAM
44	
45	For your machine, that distinction matters a lot.
46	
47	What Prolog needs at runtime
48	Even a small Prolog needs these moving parts:
49	
50	1. Term representation
51	You need to represent:
52	
53	atoms
54	
55	integers
56	
57	variables
58	
59	structures/functors
60	
61	lists
62	
63	Most implementations use tagged words/cells so the runtime can distinguish ref/int/atom/structure/list-like cells efficiently. The WAM literature is built around that style of representation. 
64	
65	2. Unification
66	This is the heart of Prolog. You need:
67	
68	dereferencing variable chains
69	
70	binding unbound vars
71	
72	structure/arity matching
73	
74	optional occurs-check
75	
76	In practice, most Prologs optimize by omitting the full occurs-check by default. The runtime then relies on trailing and heap management instead of insisting on that stronger semantics. 
77	
78	3. Backtracking
79	You need to save enough state to try the next clause when a goal fails:
80	
81	program position / next alternative
82	
83	environment / local variables
84	
85	heap top
86	
87	trail top
88	
89	This is typically stored in choice points. WAM-style systems also keep a trail so variable bindings can be undone during backtracking. 
90	
91	4. Control stack / environments
92	For non-tail calls, local variables and continuation info need to live somewhere. WAM-style systems distinguish heap, stack/environment, and trail; simpler educational systems sometimes blur these boundaries. 
93	
94	5. Some indexing
95	Even a primitive “index on first argument if atom/functor is known” helps a lot. Serious systems go farther, but you can start very small. Indexing is one of the major performance levers in practical Prolog runtimes. 
96	
97	6. Memory reclamation
98	A practical Prolog eventually wants garbage collection, but a first system can often get away with:
99	
100	resetting heap to saved choicepoint on backtrack
101	
102	no GC initially
103	
104	perhaps arena-style reclaim between top-level queries
105	
106	GC becomes more important once you want long-running sessions and richer data lifetimes. 
107	
108	What this means on COR24
109	Your constraints actually point toward a very specific conclusion.
110	
111	Good news
112	Prolog’s core execution model does not require divide or floating point. A pure integer-only Prolog is completely normal for an initial implementation. Arithmetic predicates can start tiny: is, =:=, <, >, +, -, *, maybe mod later, and you can skip floats entirely. That aligns well with classic compact Prolog subsets and teaching implementations. 
113	
114	Bad news
115	The 3 GPR limit makes a classic register-rich WAM less natural. The traditional WAM uses registers heavily for argument passing and temporary term-building/unification paths. You can still implement it, but it becomes more like a stackified WAM or memory-heavy abstract machine, not a register-friendly one. 
116	
117	That pushes you toward:
118	
119	a small interpreter, or
120	
121	a small custom bytecode VM, not a full classic WAM first
122	
123	Recommended architecture choices
124	Here are the realistic options, in order.
125	
126	Option A — PL/SW direct interpreter
127	Implement a small Prolog interpreter directly in PL/SW.
128	
129	High-level design
130	parser reads clauses into internal term structures
131	
132	runtime stores database of predicates
133	
134	evaluator runs goals depth-first, left-to-right
135	
136	unifier manipulates heap terms and variable refs
137	
138	explicit stacks:
139	
140	goal stack
141	
142	choicepoint stack
143	
144	trail stack
145	
146	heap
147	
148	Why this fits COR24
149	Because PL/SW sounds close to a systems language / portable high-level assembler, you can explicitly manage:
150	
151	tagged 24-bit cells
152	
153	stack/heap layout
154	
155	compact structs
156	
157	hand-tuned backtracking paths
158	
159	And because COR24 has few registers, a direct interpreter lets you keep most state in memory rather than forcing a register-oriented abstract machine.

376	Typical historical bootstrap patterns
377	Pattern 1: Implementation in another systems language
378	A Prolog is first implemented in C/Pascal/assembly, then maybe later rewritten partly in Prolog or in its own compiler language. That is common historically because the runtime is low-level.

381	Very common in language work:
382	
383	first get a meta-interpreter or simple clause interpreter working

387	later add indexing and optimizations

390	A host-side tool parses Prolog and emits abstract machine code; target only needs the VM. This is often the most practical embedded route.

743	So, what if I wrote an emulator for a WAM-friendly machine with many registers, that ran on top of COR24's 3 registers (using the stack or stacks).  The COR24 would be like a microcode engine, the VM would be closer to what Prolog needs.  Should I create a PL/SW emulator layer for this or enhance my p-code VM (seems unnatural to add registers to a stack-based VM, though).   Education and some practical use-cases are the goal, performance is not a high priority for this target ISA.
744	
745	Thought for a couple of seconds
746	Yes — for your goals, this is a good idea.
747	
748	You are really asking whether to:
749	
750	force Prolog into a runtime shaped like COR24, or
751	
752	put a more Prolog-shaped abstract machine on top of COR24 and let COR24 act as the microcoded substrate.
753	
754	For education and practical experimentation, option 2 is often the better architecture.
755	
756	The key question is not “Is this efficient?” but:
757	
758	Will the extra VM make the Prolog implementation simpler, clearer, and easier to evolve?
759	
760	For your use case, I think the answer is yes.
761	
762	Restating the design problem
763	You have:
764	
765	a real target with 24-bit words
766	
767	3 general-purpose registers
768	
769	no divide
770	
771	no float
772	
773	existing toolchains in PL/SW, Pascal/p-code VM, and related hosted tooling
774	
775	You want:
776	
777	a clean-room Prolog
778	
779	something educational
780	
781	something usable enough to run nontrivial examples
782	
783	performance that is “nice if present,” but not the top priority
784	
785	So the architecture should optimize for:
786	
787	conceptual clarity
788	
789	easy debugging
790	
791	fidelity to Prolog implementation ideas
792	
793	portability inside your COR24 ecosystem
794	
795	room to grow into a more WAM-like system
796	
797	That makes a layered design very attractive.
798	
799	My short answer
800	I would not extend the existing p-code VM to grow fake registers.
801	That feels like the wrong abstraction.
802	
803	I would create a new PL/SW abstract machine specifically for logic programming.
804	Think of it as:
805	
806	L0: COR24 hardware / emulator
807	
808	L1: a register-rich logic-engine VM
809	
810	L2: Prolog compiler or interpreter targeting that VM
811	
812	That is the cleanest route.
813	
814	Why a new VM layer makes sense
815	A Prolog runtime wants a machine model with concepts like:
816	
817	argument registers
818	
819	temporary registers
820	
821	heap pointer
822	
823	trail pointer
824	
825	choice point pointer
826	
827	environment pointer
828	
829	continuation / program counter
830	
831	unification modes
832	
833	clause entry / alternative entry
834	
835	A stack-oriented p-code VM is a reasonable fit for:
836	
837	Pascal
838	
839	BASIC
840	
841	expression evaluation
842	
843	procedural languages with nested calls
844	
845	But Prolog does not naturally feel like “evaluate expression stack, call subroutine, return value.”
846	It feels more like:
847	
848	build and inspect tagged terms
849	
850	match arguments
851	
852	bind variables
853	
854	save failure continuations
855	
856	unwind bindings
857	
858	resume alternatives
859	
860	That is a very different machine shape.
861	
862	So yes, trying to “grow registers” inside a stack VM is possible, but it tends to become awkward because you are bending the p-code model into something it was not designed for.
863	
864	Why this is historically reasonable
865	This is actually very much in the spirit of language implementation history.
866	
867	Many languages became practical by introducing a machine model that matched the language better than the host machine did:
868	
869	Pascal p-code machines
870	
871	Smalltalk bytecode VMs
872	
873	Lisp machines / SECD-like models
874	
875	Prolog’s WAM and related abstract machines
876	
877	So “COR24 as microcode substrate, Logic VM as target machine” is a sound idea.
878	
879	It is also educationally stronger, because it lets you study two things separately:
880	
881	How Prolog wants to run
882	
883	How to emulate that cleanly on a constrained substrate
884	
885	That separation is valuable.
886	
887	The main architectural options
888	Option A — Direct Prolog on COR24
889	Implement runtime structures directly in PL/SW and interpret clauses.
890	
891	Benefits
892	fewest layers
893	
894	easy to reason about low-level details
895	
896	no second VM to design
897	
898	Drawbacks
899	the implementation is shaped too much by COR24’s limitations
900	
901	harder to reason about “classic Prolog machine” concepts
902	
903	risk of scattered complexity in the engine
904	
905	This is still viable, but less elegant if your goal includes understanding/teaching Prolog implementation structure.
906	
907	Option B — Extend p-code VM for Prolog
908	You could add:
909	
910	a register file in memory
911	
912	extra p-code instructions to access pseudo-registers
913	
914	maybe trail/choicepoint primitives
915	
916	Benefits
917	reuse existing VM, loader, tools
918	
919	less new infrastructure
920	
921	Drawbacks
922	abstraction mismatch
923	
924	stack VM semantics fight with Prolog control model
925	
926	register emulation becomes bolted-on rather than first-class
927	
928	you may end up with “p-code plus weird exceptions”
929	
930	This is the route I would avoid unless reuse is overwhelmingly important.
931	
932	Option C — New logic-oriented VM on top of COR24
933	This is the one I recommend.
934	
935	Benefits
936	clean model
937	
938	WAM-ish structure without needing full WAM complexity
939	
940	easy to teach
941	
942	easy to instrument
943	
944	decouples Prolog semantics from COR24 awkwardness
945	
946	can evolve from interpreter-like to compiled execution
947	
948	Drawbacks
949	more up-front design
950	
951	one more assembler / loader / debugger layer
952	
953	performance overhead of emulation
954	
955	Given that performance is not your top priority, these drawbacks are acceptable.
956	
957	Should it be “WAM-friendly” or literally WAM?
958	I would strongly suggest:
959	
960	Make it WAM-friendly, not a literal textbook WAM.
961	A true classic WAM carries a lot of historical baggage and optimization assumptions. On your system, you do not need to be faithful to every traditional detail.
962	
963	Instead, design a small logic abstract machine with WAM-like ideas:
964	
965	explicit register file
966	
967	heap
968	
969	trail
970	
971	choicepoint stack
972	
973	environment stack
974	
975	code area
976	
977	predicate tables
978	
979	term tags
980	
981	instructions for get/put/unify/call/proceed/fail/backtrack
982	
983	But feel free to simplify.
984	
985	For example:
986	
987	fewer register classes
988	
989	stackified temporaries
990	
991	simpler indexing
992	
993	simpler instruction encoding
994	
995	no fancy optimization passes initially
996	
997	Think “mini-WAM for education and portability.”
998	
999	What kind of registers should this VM have?
1000	Do not model a large hardware-like register set just because WAM papers have lots of named registers.
1001	
1002	Instead define only what your implementation actually needs.
1003	
1004	A good starting point:
1005	
1006	Architectural registers
1007	These are special machine registers:
1008	
1009	HP — heap pointer
1010	
1011	TR — trail top
1012	
1013	CP — continuation pointer
1014	
1015	BP — choice point pointer
1016	
1017	EP — environment pointer
1018	
1019	PC — program counter
1020	
1021	FAIL — next failure continuation / alt entry
1022	
1023	maybe MODE — read/write mode for unification
1024	
1025	General argument/temp registers
1026	Then define a small bank:
1027	
1028	A0..A7 — argument registers
1029	
1030	X0..X7 — temporaries
1031	
1032	You do not need 256 registers.
1033	Even 8+8 may be more than enough for a first system.
1034	
1035	If desired, collapse them further:
1036	
1037	R0..R15
1038	
1039	But keeping argument registers distinct is educationally nice.
1040	
1041	Internal implementation detail
1042	On COR24, these “registers” are just entries in a memory block.
1043	
1044	So your VM instruction interpreter will do things like:
1045	
1046	load register slot from VM state area
1047	
1048	manipulate it
1049	
1050	store back
1051	
1052	That is perfectly fine.
1053	
1054	How should COR24 implement those registers?
1055	Use a VM state block in memory, not the COR24 call stack alone.
1056	
1057	That is important.
1058	
1059	Good design
1060	Have a fixed memory layout like:
1061	
1062	code area
1063	
1064	atom/functor table
1065	
1066	clause metadata
1067	
1068	register file
1069	
1070	heap
1071	
1072	trail
1073	
1074	environment stack
1075	
1076	choicepoint stack
1077	
1078	And let the VM interpreter keep pointers into these regions.
1079	
1080	Why not “just use the stack”?
1081	Because Prolog already naturally wants multiple logical stacks/areas:
1082	
1083	environment stack
1084	
1085	choicepoint stack
1086	
1087	trail
1088	
1089	heap
1090	
1091	If you use one undifferentiated COR24 stack for everything, debugging becomes painful and semantics blur together.
1092	
1093	So yes, COR24 can microcode the VM, but the VM should still expose distinct logical storage regions.
1094	
1095	Should the emulator layer be in PL/SW?
1096	Yes. I think PL/SW is the right place for this layer.
1097	
1098	Why PL/SW fits
1099	low-level control
1100	
1101	can model packed records / cells
1102	
1103	can do explicit memory management
1104	
1105	matches your “portable high-level assembler” mindset
1106	
1107	cleaner long-term identity than Pascal for this subsystem
1108	
1109	good fit for writing an emulator / abstract machine runtime
1110	
1111	Also, if your end goal includes a Prolog clean-room ecosystem inside your COR24 world, PL/SW gives that project a stronger architectural center.
1112	
1113	Why not Pascal/p-code for the VM?
1114	Pascal on p-code is still useful, but more as one of these:
1115	
1116	a prototype implementation
1117	
1118	a host-side compiler
1119	
1120	a reference test harness
1121	
1122	maybe a term parser / clause compiler
1123	
1124	It is less attractive as the long-term home of the logic VM itself because:
1125	
1126	p-code is already an abstraction for procedural computation
1127	
1128	you would be building another abstraction mismatch on top of it
1129	
1130	it makes the logic machine feel less native
1131	
1132	So I would keep p-code as a possible tooling language, not the runtime foundation.
1133	
1134	Best layered architecture
1135	Here is the architecture I would recommend.
1136	
1137	Layer 0 — COR24
1138	Your real target ISA and emulator.
1139	
1140	Layer 1 — Logic Abstract Machine (LAM)
1141	Written in PL/SW.
1142	
1143	This machine has:
1144	
1145	a code interpreter
1146	
1147	a register file
1148	
1149	heap/trail/env/choicepoint memory
1150	
1151	term operations
1152
